    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines offers a small business rewards program, known as the AAdvantage Business program. This is a great way to earn extra rewards for your travel on American, including qualifying for bonus Loyalty Points and miles.

    Sources indicate that best of all, eligibility for the program is surprisingly simple, assuming you have the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more). There’s often even a bonus for fresh AAdvantage Business members, making it even more rewarding.

    In this post, I’d like to take a look at all of the details of the AAdvantage Business program, as many people find it to be quite complicated. Note that AAdvantage Business was released in 2023, replacing the previous American Business Extra program, which no longer exists.

    AAdvantage Business is the name of American Airlines’ business rewards program. This allows you to earn extra rewards in a business account, in addition to the rewards you can earn through your own AAdvantage account. Best of all, you have quite a bit of flexibility in terms of distributing the rewards. Let’s go over the details of how this works.

    Industry observers note that the AAdvantage Business program has a pretty straightforward rewards structure, as it rewards members with both Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles. With the AAdvantage Business program, you earn the following rewards, which will post within 72 hours of an eligible flight:.

    Let me emphasize that business travelers only earn Loyalty Points through AAdvantage Business when the business is at the moment eligible to transfer miles, and that requires either having the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, or having at least five unique travelers who have credited flights to the AAdvantage Business account, totaling at least $5,000 in flight revenue, over the course of a year (the credit card method is obviously easier).

    Just to clarify a few additional points about AAdvantage Business rewards:.

    These rewards are all in addition to the standard rewards that AAdvantage members receive:.

    Industry observers note that just to be crystal clear, an Executive Platinum member ordinarily earns 11 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on airfare, while if enrolled in the AAdvantage Business program, they’d earn 12 Loyalty Points per dollar spent. There’s no reason to leave those bonus rewards on the table!

    Industry observers note that in order to be eligible to participate in the AAdvantage Business program, you need to have a business in the United States or Canada with a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Business Number. Even small businesses are eligible for this program.

    The exceptions are that travel agencies, consolidators, wholesalers, and other sellers of travel, aren’t eligible to participate in AAdvantage Business. On top of that, AAdvantage Business technically can’t be used for leisure travel.

    You accrue rewards in the AAdvantage Business program without any minimums, and then you can transfer the rewards to individual members, so that they can then redeem them out of their own accounts. In order to transfer the miles in the AAdvantage Business account to an individual AAdvantage account, you need to meet one of two requirements:.

    Recent findings suggest that the AAdvantage Business program creates a huge incentive to get the Citi AAdvantage Business Card. That’s because just having the card allows many people to unlock the value of the AAdvantage Business program — there’s no need to actually use the card for your spending, but just having it is all that’s needed to redeem AAdvantage Business program rewards with no minimum on the number of travelers or revenue.

    There are several potentially useful perks to this card, and on top of that, the card is offering a great welcome bonus, which is the reason that I applied for the card (and got approved), as that’s a nice incentive, beyond the value of access to the AAdvantage Business program.

    It’s worth understanding how closely this card is actually integrated into the AAdvantage Business program:.

    For American frequent flyers with a small business, this creates a strong incentive to get the card. The card has a reasonable annual fee that’s waived the first year, and just having the card will allow many people to earn a sizable number of bonus miles.

    In a recent development, if you’re curious about how the AAdvantage Business program works in practice, let me share some screenshots, for those who are more visual. Once you have an AAdvantage Business account, you’ll automatically become the travel manager for the account, and that means you can invite others to join your account (these should be people who work for your firm, but there’s no verification process, as far as I know).

    According to recent reports, I should also mention that you can designate others to be travel managers as well, so that they can also invite others, transfer miles to people, etc. Travel managers must also be AAdvantage members who are adults and are residents of the United States or Canada.

    To go through the process of inviting others to join your account, you’ll want to click “Invite people,” and then once they accept your invitation, they’ll show up on your account.

    If someone’s AAdvantage account is linked to an AAdvantage Business program account, you’ll see that when you go to make a booking on aa.com, you’ll be asked for your “Travel type,” and can select “Business” or “Personal.” If you select “Business,” you’ll see that the firm name populates, and you can select the name of the traveler.

    Note that AAdvantage Business bookings are limited to one passenger, so if you have multiple people traveling, you’ll need to book as separate reservations. Also, to state the obvious, AAdvantage award tickets don’t qualify.

    It has been revealed that while the Loyalty Points from flights will post directly to the AAdvantage account of the member, the redeemable miles will post to the AAdvantage Business program account (the same is true for miles earned on the Citi AAdvantage Business Card). If you want to redeem miles, the only option is to transfer them to individual members, as you can’t redeem the miles directly out of the AAdvantage Business account.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re eligible to transfer those miles, you’ll see the mileage balance listed, plus a “Transfer miles” button. There’s also a dashboard that highlights your eligible number of travelers and eligible spending. However, as you can see above, I’ve met the transfer conditions even though I haven’t met the required threshold, since I have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

    The process of transferring miles is super easy. You’ll just enter how many miles you want to transfer, and who you want to transfer them to, and then they should post to the AAdvantage account instantly.

    My general take on the AAdvantage Business program is as follows:.

    The program basically offers an incremental 1.5% return on your American spending, since you earn one extra AAdvantage mile per dollar spent, and based on my miles & points valuations, those are worth 1.5 cents each. On top of that, the program offers an incremental Loyalty Point per dollar spent — that will have no value to some, while it will have significant value to others, depending on the extent to which you’re pursuing status in the coming year.

    It is interesting the extent to which American has basically given up on corporate travel. American’s priority is getting people to book direct and keeping distribution costs as low as possible. So this program is intended as the major incentive for most small businesses.

    In a recent development, american Airlines offers the AAdvantage Business program. With this program, the business earns one AAdvantage mile per dollar spent on eligible airfare, while the individual traveler earns one Loyalty Point per dollar spent. In order to participate and be able to redeem miles, you need a business with at least five registered employees who have each taken at least one eligible flight, along with $5,000 in annual spending, or you need to have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

    What do you make of the AAdvantage Business program?

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. While this is still being investigated, there’s a theory as to what happened, given what all passengers had in common….

    On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA). Both flights were operated by the Airbus A330-900neo, with as many as 620 passengers onboard.

    Flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday. The flights had one thing in common, which is that between them, dozens of passengers became ill.

    It has been revealed that the illnesses onboard were so bad that a “MANV 25” response was triggered at Frankfurt Airport. That’s a German emergency response alert for a mass casualty incident — “Massenanfall von Verletzten” (though fortunately there were no fatalities here).

    Passengers onboard were screened by medical teams, and one person on each flight was taken to a local hospital, while others are being monitored.

    Sources indicate that it’s not uncommon to hear stories of multiple people becoming sick on flights. Sometimes it’s a fume event, sometimes it could be a case of food poisoning (though it doesn’t usually happen that fast), etc. So what’s going on here, that people on two separate Condor flights became ill?

    Well, the passengers on these two flights had one thing in common — they all came off the AidaBella cruise ship in La Romana, and then these flights were sold as part of the cruise package.

    So while this is still being investigated, a norovirus outbreak on the cruise ship is believed to be the likely culprit. I’ve gotta say, an airplane seems like a pretty unpleasant place to come down with a gastrointestinal illness, so I imagine the lavatory situation onboard probably wasn’t great.

    Dozens of passengers on two separate Condor flights between the Dominican Republic and Germany around the same time became ill, triggering an emergency response at Frankfurt Airport, which included a couple of people being hospitalized.

    While it remains to be seen what caused this, the belief is that it could be some sort of a norovirus outbreak, based on the symptoms, as well as the fact that the passengers had all come off the same cruise ship. I hope everyone makes a quick recovery.

    Getting a refund for a canceled or delayed flight: What your rights are in 2026

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (165 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • Recent disruptions in U.S. air travel highlight the importance of understanding passenger refund rights.
  • Federal rules require airlines to issue refunds for canceled flights or significant delays if you choose not to travel, regardless of the cause.
  • A 'significant delay' is defined as three hours or more for domestic flights and six hours or more for international flights.
  • Refunds must be processed automatically and promptly—within seven days for credit card payments and 20 days for other payment methods.
  • Refund eligibility only applies if you decline rebooking and do not accept alternative compensation such as vouchers or miles.
  • Airlines are not required to provide compensation for meals, hotels or ground transportation unless the disruption is within their control.
  • Passengers can file a complaint with the Department of Transportation if they believe refund rules were not followed.

    House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    It has been revealed that “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., noted earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    In a recent development, when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    The committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    In a recent development, “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she stated in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack remarked that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack noted in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., stated everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he stated at Thursday’s meeting.

    Qatar Airways Airbus A321LRs With Flat Bed Business Class Launching Soon

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds.
    • Qatar Airways currently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order.
    • Recent findings suggest that the expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds. The airline will be introducing a “mini-Qsuite” type product on these planes, and we’ve now learned exactly when this latest premium narrow body jet will enter service.

    Qatar Airways currently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order. This includes 10 A321LRs and 40 A321neos — both of those are latest generation aircraft, with the A321LR featuring additional range.

    Recent findings suggest that the expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026. The 10 A321LRs should join the fleet pretty swiftly, and will then be followed by the A321neos. The A321LRs will be configured with 160 seats, including 16 business class seats and 144 economy class seats.

    Sources indicate that the A321LR has a maximum range of 4,000 nautical miles, so it can be used for many destinations in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Below is a map showing the rough range from Doha (though in reality it won’t be quite as far, accounting for winds, fuel reserves, etc.).

    Now, for those paying close attention, I should acknowledge that Qatar Airways briefly flew six leased, all-economy A321neos, but those were just intended as a temporary solution, and are now flying for Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is running an interesting operation.

    In a recent development, qatar Airways’ A321neo-family aircraft order goes back a long time, and involved a lot of drama. The order was first declared in 2011, then the airline reconfirmed and upsized it in 2017. However, then former Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker got into a fight with Airbus over A350 production quality, and refused to take delivery of any Airbus planes.

    That turned into a massive court battle, which was eventually resolved. But in the process, Qatar Airways lost all of its Airbus delivery slots, which is why these planes are coming way later than initially expected.

    Qatar Airways has been promising all along that it would introduce some sort of a next generation flat bed business class product on its Airbus A321LRs. As you’d expect, business class seats on narrow bodies sometimes differ from those on wide bodies, due to differing cabin constraints.

    What can we expect onboard these Qatar Airways A321LRs in business class? Executive Traveller quotes Qatar Airways CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater as saying that the upcoming business class product will be based on the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform.

    These planes will boast 16 business class seats, in a 1-1 configuration. This product offers reverse herringbone seats, and Qatar Airways looks to have doors at each seat as well, of course with its customized finishes.

    According to recent reports, the launch customer for the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform was Air France on its A350s. However, that’s the wide body version of the seat, which is modified from the narrow body version.

    When it comes to the narrow body version of the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, ITA Airways was the launch customer, on its A321neos.

    This is also the product that Etihad is installing on its A321LRs. ITA Airways and Etihad don’t have doors in business class, but Qatar Airways does initiative to offer it. Etihad also markets the first row of the cabin as first class (and that has doors), but I wouldn’t expect Qatar Airways to do something similar.

    This is about as good as narrow body business class seats get, as it’s generally preferred to the herringbone seats you’ll find on other carriers, like JetBlue A321LRs, American A321XLRs, etc.

    Qatar Airways now seems pretty certain about the delivery of its upcoming Airbus A321LRs, as the airline has officially put the first routes on sale, as flagged by AeroRoutes:.

    When you pull up the above flights, you’ll now see the seat map for the A321LR, which confirms the 16-seat business class cabin.

    Recent findings suggest that in the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first of 10 Airbus A321LRs. This will be the first custom designed next generation narrow body that the airline takes delivery of. We knew the airline would offer flat bed seats on these planes, and now we have the details of that.

    The airline has gone with the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, the same product you’ll find on similar planes of Etihad and ITA Airways. However, unlike those airlines, Qatar Airways will have doors in business class. The planes will enter service by very early 2027, flying from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich.

    What do you make of Qatar Airways’ upcoming A321LRs, and the planned interiors?

    American Blocking Domestic Saver Awards Close To Departure (Within Six Days)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major latest restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).
    • With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure.
    • In a recent development, historically, American has been by far the best of the “significant three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major latest restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).

    With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure. Initially, all domestic nonstop saver awards within six days of departure were pulled. In recent days, it looks like American has expanded this to all domestic connecting itineraries as well, so I’d like to cover those details (thanks to azbobcat for flagging this).

    In a recent development, historically, American has been by far the best of the “significant three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights. American actually releases a good amount of saver award seats across cabins, and it’s one of the things that makes AAdvantage better than the competition.

    Recent findings suggest that however, in May 2026, we saw American introduce a major change to how it releases award space to partner frequent flyer programs. Long story short, American started blocking all nonstop, domestic saver award availability, for flights within six days (exactly 144 hours) of departure.

    As soon as a flight gets to the point where it’s 144 hours until departure, you’ll see that the airline “turns off” its saver fare classes — I’m referring specifically to the “U” (saver business class award) and “T” (saver economy award) fare classes, which show up when searching on ExpertFlyer, for example.

    Initially, this applied exclusively to nonstop, domestic award tickets, as connecting itineraries and all international itineraries (including short haul international ones) weren’t impacted by this. However, this seems to have now expanded to domestic connecting itineraries as well.

    So any wholly domestic itinerary exclusively on American is no longer bookable at the saver level within six days of departure. International itineraries continue to be bookable within six days of departure, whether traveling nonstop or with a connection.

    What would cause American to suddenly “shut off” saver awards for domestic routes within days of departure?

    What’s interesting here is that the implications for AAdvantage members are limited. Yes, American has shut off awards in the saver fare classes, but that’s not to say that American isn’t making reasonably priced awards available within days of departure. American has long used some kind of dynamic award pricing concept for its own flights, regardless of whether or not there’s saver availability.

    It’s just that any awards in the official saver fare buckets aren’t available, and therefore aren’t bookable with points belonging to partner programs.

    Industry observers note that so it sure seems to me that the intent here is to block award availability for those booking through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club. It goes without saying that I absolutely hate this restriction, as someone who “funds” a vast majority of my domestic American travel using Atmos Rewards points. At the same time, I also have to say that I can’t blame American for this change, as the airline has just made it too easy.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve been booking basically all my travel directly into American first class using Atmos Rewards points — I just set ExpertFlyer availability alerts for “U” class, it opens up a vast majority of the time, and then I book. It’s not surprising that American finally got a bit savvier.

    Recent findings suggest that american is now blocking all saver awards within exactly six days of departure for all domestic itineraries. This means within that timeframe, there’s no “U” or “T” availability, which corresponds to the saver business and economy award fare buckets, respectively. Initially this only applied to nonstop flights, while now it also applies to connecting itineraries.

    According to recent reports, for American AAdvantage members, the implications are limited, since American can still make reasonably priced awards available, just not formally in those fare buckets. The practical implications here are that partner programs just don’t have access to these award seats close to departure anymore.

    What do you make of American’s six day rule on award tickets?

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Sources indicate that how did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content?
    • Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    President Trump makes no secret of his desire to punish broadcasters whose content he dislikes. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr is a willing partner, going so far as to threaten the licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations with an early renewal proceeding. This highly unusual move (purportedly for unlawful discrimination) followed President Trump’s demand that ABC and NBC affiliates lose their broadcast licenses for unfavorable coverage of him.

    Sources indicate that how did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content? Two features of federal law enable this abuse: a vague public interest standard open to broad, subjective interpretation, and an archaic equal time rule.

    Brian A. Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    On “The Public Interest Demands Free Speech for Broadcasters”.

    Breeze Airways Adds 6 New Cities & 9 Routes: See Full List Now

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Breeze Airways is preparing to introduce six destinations to its growing network, with nine nonstop routes launching between December 2026 and July 2027.
    • It has been revealed that the additions highlight Breeze's strategy of connecting underserved domestic markets while expanding its international presence, particularly from Tampa International Airport (TPA).
    • In a recent development, the six additions represent several distinct markets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Breeze Airways is preparing to introduce six destinations to its growing network, with nine nonstop routes launching between December 2026 and July 2027. The additions include Boston, Buffalo, Latrobe, St. Thomas, Montego Bay, and Santo Domingo. Four were included in the airline's October network expansion announcement, while services to St. Thomas and Montego Bay were declared earlier.

    It has been revealed that the additions highlight Breeze's strategy of connecting underserved domestic markets while expanding its international presence, particularly from Tampa International Airport (TPA). The Florida airport is also becoming increasingly vital to the airline's overall network, with it overtaking Raleigh-Durham as the airline's busiest airport according to schedule data running until August 2027.

    In a recent development, the six additions represent several distinct markets. Boston, Buffalo and Latrobe are on the US mainland, while Montego Bay in Jamaica and Santo Domingo in the Dominican Republic expand Breeze's international reach. St. Thomas, meanwhile, is part of the US Virgin Islands and is therefore a domestic destination, albeit a further expansion of the carrier's Caribbean network. It also brings Breeze's planned network to a total of 95 destinations.

    In a recent development, services to St. Thomas and Montego Bay will begin in December, followed by Latrobe in February, Boston in May, Santo Domingo in June, and Buffalo later that month. The latest published schedules, alongside Breeze's October announcement, confirm the following nine routes and planned frequencies:.

    Recent findings suggest that boston–Myrtle Beach will have the highest frequency, operating daily, with onward same-aircraft service to Akron-Canton. Most of the other routes will operate twice-weekly, consistent with Breeze's strategy of providing nonstop connections between underserved markets.

    Industry observers note that latrobe provides a clear example of Breeze identifying an opportunity following another airline's departure. ABC News reported how Arnold Palmer Regional Airport (LBE), approximately 40 miles (64 km) east of Pittsburgh, lost its only scheduled commercial carrier when Spirit Airlines ceased operations in May. Breeze's arrival will restore scheduled passenger flights, beginning with Myrtle Beach in February and Orlando in May. It is particularly good news for the airport, which has been undergoing a terminal expansion project to accommodate future growth.

    Buffalo represents a different opportunity, with Breeze launching three routes within four days. Raleigh–Durham International Airport (RDU) will receive four weekly departures from late June, while Myrtle Beach and Charleston will each receive two. The RDU connection is particularly notable given that the North Carolina airport became Breeze's busiest earlier this year. With the addition of Buffalo, Breeze will now fly to 43 destinations from its North Carolina base.

    Sources indicate that myrtle Beach is another major beneficiary, appearing in three of the nine new routes. Breeze is adding 11 nonstop connections there during 2027, taking its network to 25 destinations in total and positioning it to become the airport's largest airline by seats and destinations. Cirium schedule data also shows that between now and next summer, Breeze's departures from Myrtle Beach will have risen by 86%, making it the second-fastest growing airport in the network after Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

    Breeze's busiest airport has changed repeatedly as its network has rapidly expanded. For the longest time, Orlando International Airport (MCO) was the undisputed leader, before RDU overtook it earlier this year. But looking forward at available schedules through August 2027, Tampa has emerged to claim the top spot. Its 7,390 scheduled departures over that period represents a 72% year-over-year increase.

    Recent findings suggest that tampa's rise up the rankings is especially striking because it's not like Breeze's other bases are standing still. Raleigh-Durham will grow by 45% and Orlando by 31% over that same period. And a little further back, Fort Lauderdale is set to grow by a whopping 259% (albeit off a much smaller base) as Breeze joins JetBlue in filling the void left by Spirit Airlines.

    Recent findings suggest that tampa's international expansion is a big driver of Breeze's growth at the airport. The airline introduced its first international service from the airport to Nassau in June, followed by Punta Cana in July and San José in October. St. Thomas and Montego Bay arrive in December, while Santo Domingo rolls out with year-round service in June next year, ensuring that Tampa has also become Breeze's largest base for international operations.

    Southwest Airlines Plus Card Review: Modest Benefits For A Low Annual Fee

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees).
    • In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that southwest Airlines and Chase have a great portfolio of co-branded credit cards at a variety of “price points” (and by that I mean annual fees). In this post, I’d like to take a closer look at the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card, which is Southwest Airlines’ lowest annual fee credit card.

    In my Southwest Plus Card review, I’ll cover the benefits and explain why now is a good time to consider this card if you want to use credit card spending to earn the Companion Pass. I’ll also explain why other Southwest cards can be better, and share a great alternative to earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points altogether.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card.

    Before I get into my Southwest Plus Card review, here are some of the key card details:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Plus Card’s pros and cons:.

    Let’s take a look at the Southwest Plus Card‘s welcome bonus, annual fee, and eligibility rules, as these are some of the most important factors to take into account if you’re considering applying.

    The Southwest Plus Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is one of the higher bonuses I’ve seen on this card recently, making now a particularly good time to apply.

    Sources indicate that rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $960.

    In terms of Southwest credit card eligibility, the card isn’t available to anyone who presently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, keep in mind the general restrictions for Chase card approvals, including the 5/24 rule. However, there are increasing data points of this no longer being consistently enforced.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    You’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for this card now if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Recent findings suggest that now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    Recent findings suggest that this change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only new rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    The Southwest Plus Card has a $99 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost.

    $99 is the lowest annual fee of any Southwest Airlines credit card. Looking at the high end, Southwest’s personal cards have annual fees of up to $229, and Southwest’s business cards have annual fees of up to $299.

    The Southwest Plus Card has no foreign transaction fees, so it’s a solid card to use for purchases abroad.

    As far as the Southwest Plus Card‘s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:.

    Since I value Southwest Rapid Rewards points at 1.2 cents each, I think you get an effective return of 2.4% on purchases that qualify for 2x points, and a 1.2% return on everything else.

    In a recent development, it’s nice that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Plus, a few of the non-Southwest bonus categories have an annual cap, which limits how useful this card is for maximizing your return on gas station and grocery store purchases.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Plus Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    In a recent development, starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    Recent findings suggest that one great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. However, this is also Southwest’s lowest annual fee card, so it doesn’t have the most benefits. What are the ongoing perks of having this card?

    Recent findings suggest that the Southwest Plus Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. So with just one roundtrip flight per year, this benefit can almost offset the annual fee.

    It has been revealed that southwest now charges for seat selection, so it’s helpful that the Southwest Plus Card includes complimentary standard seat selection starting 48 hours out from departure. This perk is based on availability, and it could save you around $20 to $40 per flight.

    Another Southwest benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

    Each year on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 10% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this discount excludes Basic fares.

    Recent findings suggest that on your Southwest Plus Card cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 3,000 bonus points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you’ll typically need 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book. In other words, those 3,000 Rapid Rewards points should get you around $36 worth of airfare on Southwest annually.

    As part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Plus Card.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

    The Southwest Plus Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the great features of Chase cards is access to Chase Offers, which provides savings on purchases with all kinds of retailers. This program has saved me a significant amount of money.

    The Southwest Plus Card is a solid entry-level airline credit card. If you want a credit card from Southwest and want an annual fee as low as possible, then this card could make sense to you.

    Sources indicate that you’ll receive a 3,000-point bonus on your cardmember anniversary every year, and 25% savings on inflight purchases. The free checked bag benefit can save you $90 on a roundtrip and the complimentary standard seat selection benefit can add up rapidly after a few flights. These perks can more than justify the annual fee, and that’s not even accounting for the massive welcome bonus.

    However, there are other options that I think can make more sense.

    If your main reason for considering the Southwest Rapid Rewards Plus Card is to earn points for Southwest award flights, you might be better off skipping a Southwest co-branded credit card altogether and just earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points. You can transfer Chase points to Southwest to book flights, and cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) have stronger earning categories and benefits overall.

    You can also redeem Ultimate Rewards points with other travel partners, not just Southwest, so this option gives you more flexibility.

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step up from the Southwest Plus Card, with a $149 annual fee. Here’s a look at its key perks:.

    There’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (learn more), the most premium personal Southwest card with a $229 annual fee. If you want as many Southwest perks as possible, this is a better pick.

    The Southwest Priority Card’s main perks include:.

    So you’re getting a higher return of 4.8% on Southwest spending on the Priority Card, based on my valuations, and better complimentary seat selection and upgrade options.

    Recent findings suggest that if you want a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card in place of or in addition to a personal card, I highly recommend considering the Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). The Southwest Performance Business Card offers the following benefits, which make it the best Southwest credit card, in my opinion:.

    The Southwest Performance Business Card offers a lot of points, and more perks overall than other Southwest cards.

    According to recent reports, the Southwest Plus Card is a good entry-level credit card for someone who wants to earn Rapid Rewards points without paying a high annual fee. It’s not the most valuable Southwest credit card in the lineup, but its benefits and strong welcome bonus make it a good option at this price point.

    Breaking: Delta Is My Preferred Airline Of The “Substantial Three” US Carriers (Hear Me Out)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire.
    • This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.
    • Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’ve never been one to take the easy road, so I thought I’d bite the bullet and talk about my love for Delta in what you might call a baptism of fire. Before I jump in, I’m not here screaming that Delta is the best US airline. Far from it. Rather, I’m explaining why, as someone who is not based in the US, Delta is my go-to airline.

    This year, Delta has nudged up to fourth most-flown of the 94 airlines I’ve tried out over the years, and I’d like to share a little bit about why.

    Starting from the ground, I am a big fan of what Delta is doing with its lounges. Stepping inside one of Delta’s newer Sky Clubs, you feel like you’re in the lobby bar of a luxury hotel rather than the corporate canteen-style spaces offered by competitors.

    I know these newer lounges aren’t in every airport yet — Honolulu (HNL) is a notable exception — but lately I’ve found myself enjoying them before the majority of my latest Delta flights departing from a US airport.

    Don’t get me started on the Delta One Lounges: I’ve visited locations at LAX and JFK, and these are without a doubt my favorite airline lounges in the US.

    Stepping onboard, I actually like the planes. In recent times, I’ve flown mainly on its Airbus A320 family aircraft, a few Boeing 757s (which I love), and once on a Boeing 767-300 from Honolulu to LAX.

    I like how they’ve all had seatback screens, I’ve never had an problem using my SkyMiles account to access the fast free WiFi (it’s decent, even though it’s not Starlink), and I’ve never felt uncomfortable on one of Delta’s planes.

    I also have to say, I’ve always had pleasant, if not better-than-your-average service when flying Delta.

    Sources indicate that I love a good redemption as much as the next frequent flyer. However, our credit cards in the UK earn us far fewer points than those in the US, so for me, redeeming points is the exception, not the norm.

    Sources indicate that as such, I don’t hate on Delta’s SkyMiles for its mostly sky-high redemption rates. Even if finding a one-way in Delta One from Rio or São Paulo to New York for less than 470,000 miles is almost impossible.

    Besides, I credit my Delta flights to my Flying Blue account, which is therefore home to my SkyTeam elite status and miles earned on Delta and all other SkyTeam airlines.

    Neither do I fly often enough nor have the funds to unlock top-tier status in all three alliances. Aside from the Virgin Atlantic Gold status I got from a status match and my BA Silver, which expires in April, Flying Blue is the only program whose status I’m actively chasing.

    Sources indicate that as a direct result of Air France and KLM’s membership in the SkyTeam alliance, I actively choose to fly other SkyTeam airlines, such as Delta. Also, thanks to the relationship between Delta and fellow SkyTeam member Aeroméxico, I’ve managed to find great-value cash fares on several occasions when planning travel between Mexico and Canada or the US.

    Sources indicate that I actually used to be a die-hard American boy until the BA Club was sabotaged. In terms of lounges, aircraft comfort, complimentary amenities (like seat back screens and Wi-Fi), and service, Delta has felt like an upgrade.

    For what it’s worth, if status had nothing to do with it, I’d still choose Delta.

    My experience with American, Delta, and United has mainly been on domestic flights around the US, including transcons. In fact, I’ve never flown Delta One, American Flagship, or United Polaris on long-haul international flights. Who knows, my top three could reshuffle once I’ve tried and tested each of those. Maybe I’ll have to have a word with Ben about this….

    I know Delta gets a bad rep, but honestly I have only had pleasant experiences when flying the airline over the years. As long as I’m being loyal to SkyTeam, it will remain my preference when traveling to or around the US (unless it’s from the UK; then I’m team Virgin).

    In a recent development, I’m going to make it a priority to fly each of American, Delta, and United’s best international long-haul products over the coming months. Watch this space for my thoughts on flying those for the first time, and to see whether Delta remains my US number one.

    I’m curious, what do you love or hate about Delta?

    Tech Report: Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
    • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
    • In a recent development, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, stated additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    In a recent development, senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Industry observers note that democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    According to recent reports, “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    Industry observers note that as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    As with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

    Sources indicate that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    In a recent development, “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., mentioned Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    In a recent development, as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    Recent findings suggest that the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    When To Use The Flight Attendant Call Button (And When To Skip It)

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1465 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question.
    • Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those).
    • The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To push the flight attendant call button, or not to push the flight attendant call button, that is the question. I’ll share my take, and then I’m curious to hear how OMAAT readers feel. Let’s start with some background, and then we’ll discuss best practices….

    Every airplane seat has a flight attendant call button, typically in the overhead console, right by the reading light and individual air nozzle (if the plane has those). The flight attendant call button, is, as the name suggests, a way to call a flight attendant to your seat.

    The flight attendant call button typically depicts a person with a tray, suggesting that the call button is intended for service. However, that’s not how all flight attendants interpret it, so I want to talk about that in a bit more detail.

    In most of the world, the flight attendant call button seems to work as intended. It’s a useful way to call over a flight attendant, whether you want a drink refill, or there’s some sort of an emergency.

    However, in the United States I’ve heard several flight attendants over the years announce that the call button is in fact the “emergency flight attendant call button,” advising passengers to only use it if absolutely necessary. Suffice to say that this kind of announcement isn’t approved by any airline.

    While people will often joke “well I’m happy you consider my drink request to be an emergency,” let’s talk about when it’s actually appropriate to use a flight attendant call button.

    Recent findings suggest that broadly speaking, it’s always appropriate to use the flight attendant call button for service in first & business class, especially on international airlines. You’re paying a premium for more service, and having an extra request on a long haul flight isn’t unreasonable.

    I’ll take it a step further — at top airlines, crews generally prefer that you push the call button rather than going to the galley with your request. Foreign carriers typically have thick curtains between the galley and the cabin, and you generally shouldn’t try to go into the flight attendant’s “space” without permission. They’d much rather come to you. They might be putting on some makeup or eating a meal, and don’t want to be caught off guard. So absolutely push the flight attendant call button — it’s the courteous thing to do.

    I do want to mention just one caveat — try to be respectful of the overall service flow. For example, if a cabin has 50+ business class seats and the crew is doing service with a cart and is presently in the aisle, wait until they finish that round of service before pushing the call button again, unless there’s something you absolutely need.

    When it comes to using the call button, you can’t beat Emirates first class, where you can voice or video call the crew with any requests, without them even having to come to your seat.

    Industry observers note that it’s also interesting to observe the cultural differences between airlines when it comes to service approaches. For example, in Singapore Airlines first class I generally don’t push the flight attendant call button, since even on a long haul flight, a crew member seems to pass through the cabin every 10-15 minutes throughout the flight. The service is just so proactive that I don’t find it necessary.

    Cathay Pacific first class is exactly the opposite — the crews are spectacularly reactive. That might sound sarcastic, but it’s not. On Cathay Pacific you (hopefully) won’t see a flight attendant once between meal services without calling them, and that’s so that your privacy is maximized. But if you push the call button a flight attendant will cheerily appear within seconds.

    Of course those are both airlines known for great service. You have all kinds of other airlines where flight attendants make a habit of not passing through the cabin, and when they do they almost seem to look down, to avoid making eye contact.

    Using the flight attendant call button in economy is trickier. There’s nothing inherently wrong with it, but the staffing ratio in economy is different than in first & business class, and in many cases flight attendants have to walk a lot further to your seat. Also keep in mind that on long haul flights the crew has rest periods, reducing the staffing ratio even further.

    Personally I think there’s nothing wrong with using the call button in economy:.

    Sources indicate that that being said, in economy I also think it’s more reasonable to stretch your legs and go to the galley yourself. Generally there’s a small setup with snacks and drinks, at least on long haul flights, so you can help yourself to that. Furthermore, in my experience flight attendants are typically “sitting in the open” more in economy than in business or first class, given that the volume of requests is greater.

    Recent findings suggest that the above are my general thoughts, though is the story any different on airlines in the United States? This accounts for the fact that:.

    Recent findings suggest that on US airlines I’m generally a little more hesitant to use the call button. I see what kind of a vibe the crew gives me. In general I don’t mind pushing the call button in international first & business class on a US airline, while I avoid it on domestic flights. If I get the sense that the crew takes issue with use of the call button, I of course won’t use it.

    Industry observers note that all airplane seats have individual flight attendant call buttons, though customs around using them seem to differ. In the United States, some flight attendants seem to think these buttons are just for emergencies, while outside the United States there are consistently no issues with using them for service.

    Where do you stand on using the flight attendant call button, and what has your experience been?

    With that in mind, if you were eligible for a 100% bonus and purchased 300,000 IHG One Rewards points pre-bonus, you’d receive a total of 600,000 points at a cost of $3,000, which is a rate of 0.5 cents per IHG point.

    While The Brand Latest IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), offer a 30% discount on purchased points, that benefit only applies when buying points at the normal cost, and wouldn’t be applicable here.

    In a recent development, IHG One Rewards ordinarily lets members purchase up to 150,000 points per calendar year, before any bonuses. However, during this promotion that cap has been increased to 300,000 points, pre-bonus.

    When IHG One Rewards does offer a promotion on purchased points, the 100% bonus or 50% discount is the most common offer. A 100% bonus and 50% discount give you the same price per point, so you’ll typically pay 0.5 cents per point during a promotion.

    Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

    IHG One Rewards points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you pay with an IHG credit card, you wouldn’t earn any bonus rewards, so it’s not treated as if it’s IHG spending.

    Recent findings suggest that therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See this post for more on which credit cards are best for buying points.

    It has been revealed that IHG One Rewards has dynamic award pricing, which means there’s no minimum or maximum number of points a hotel stay can cost. Rather, the cost of an award stay generally correlates somewhat to the cost of a revenue stay.

    Recent findings suggest that however, that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the same value with all hotel stays. There are many situations where you can get outsized value by buying points and then redeeming them. Let me just give a few examples, using stays I pulled up for random dates (again, pricing is dynamic, so this won’t reflect what you see every day).

    For example, the Six Senses Kyoto is bookable for 165,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $825.

    That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $1,493.

    On the other end of the spectrum, the Holiday Inn Express & Suites Tampa is bookable for 33,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $165.

    That represents massive savings over the cash cost, which is $230.

    However, this won’t always be a good deal. For example, take the Kimpton Tres Rios in Playa del Carmen is bookable for 104,000 points per night, and you could purchase those points for $520.

    That’s not a good deal compared to the cash cost, which is $429, so there you’d be better off just paying cash directly.

    Another thing to keep in mind is that select IHG co-branded credit cards offer free night awards, and those are worth up to a certain number of points. What’s great is that these free night awards can typically be topped off with points, so there could be merit to buying IHG points so that you have points with which to top off these certificates.

    You’ll get the most value from your IHG points if you have The Brand Newly introduced IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more), The New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more), and The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more).

    That’s because the cards offer a fourth night free benefit, meaning that you can book a four night award stay for the cost of three nights. This is essentially the equivalent of 25% off in increments of four nights, since you can use this benefit an unlimited number of times.

    Just to use the Six Senses Kyoto example above, if you earned 495,000 points (worth $2,475 at 0.5 cents per point), that would be enough for four nights with the fourth night free. That represents an absolutely massive discount.

    It has been revealed that IHG has over 15 hotel brands, so there are lots of options for redeeming your IHG One Rewards points. IHG points can be redeemed at the following properties, among others:.

    Recent findings suggest that everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG points to be worth 0.5 cents each, and I tend to value points pretty conservatively. So the purchase price is around what I value these points.

    Recent findings suggest that for non-elite members, IHG One Rewards points expire after 12 months of inactivity. However, any sort of points earning or redemption activity would reset the expiration of your points. Furthermore, IHG One Rewards points don’t expire for elite members in the program.

    In a recent development, keep in mind that IHG elite status is quite easy to earn. Just for having The Brand Upcoming IHG One Rewards Premier Select Credit Card (learn more) or The New IHG One Rewards Business Credit Card (learn more), you receive Platinum status, without any sort of a spending requirement.

    In a recent development, IHG One Rewards doesn’t have blackout dates on award nights, but the program does have capacity controls. What this means is that some number of standard rooms will be made available for award redemptions every night, but that doesn’t mean that all standard rooms are available for award redemptions.

    IHG One Rewards is offering a sale on purchased points. Through December 11, 2026, IHG One Rewards is offering a promotion, and members seem to be eligible for a 100% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for 0.5 cents each.

    There are instances where buying points can save you over 50% on the cost of a luxury hotel stay. I also think there’s value in having a “reserve” of IHG points, given the brand’s global footprint. You can get even more value out of buying IHG points in conjunction with a premium IHG credit card, so you can get a fourth night free on award redemptions.

    #179925. Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (558 w)

    Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government.
    • Sources indicate that fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal.
    • No doubt, with a stampede of new socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government. And here we are.

    Sources indicate that fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal. He endorsed lowering the retirement age of Medicare and adding vision, hearing, and dental coverage to the program. Additionally, he noted that the government should provide coverage for all children.

    No doubt, with a stampede of new socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.

    It has been revealed that at this point, Jeffries’s proposal is theoretical. There’s a big budgetary difference between lowering the Medicare eligibility age from its current 65 to 60, and lowering it to 50 — as Senator Kirsten Gillibrand and other senators are proposing. There are also questions about what sort of premiums, if any, would be required for near-retirees to “buy in” to the program or how generous the theoretical vision, hearing, and dental benefits would be. Filling in those blanks is the difference between a proposal that costs a few hundred billion dollars and one that costs trillions of dollars.

    Sources indicate that but it’s preposterous at this stage to start any discussion of Medicare with a suggestion that spending on the program needs to be increased rather than reined in — especially to cover a population without a high uninsured rate. Over the next decade, the federal government is projected to spend $18.5 trillion on Medicare, making it the largest expenditure apart from that other federal entitlement, Social Security. Medicare no longer collects enough money in payroll taxes to cover current benefits, let alone added benefits that cover more people. Even a more modest lowering of the retirement age to 60 would add over 7 million beneficiaries. On its current trajectory, Medicare’s trust fund (the money it is “owed” by the rest of the government from the days when it was running surpluses) would be exhausted by 2033.

    Industry observers note that medicare is a major driver of the nation’s broader fiscal problem. Already, debt held by the public has eclipsed 100 percent of gross domestic product. By the end of the decade, it is projected to reach 120 percent. By comparison, debt peaked at 106 percent during World War II. Now we are on track to exceed that number, not during a global crisis, but during an ordinary period of relative peace and prosperity. And that’s before Jeffries grabs the gavel with a massive majority behind him.

    Perhaps more concerning, President Trump indicated last week that he may be game for some compromise proposal. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care,” he noted.

    If Trump is serious and actually considers cutting a deal with Democrats to expand Medicare, congressional Republicans should fight it at all costs.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.
